title: Pediatric septic shock: how much fluid

bedside.infusions: Balanced crystalloid given {round(totalKg)} mL/kg ({round(totalKg * weight)} mL); epinephrine step {epiStep}

banner.text: Intubated for pulmonary edema after fluid overload.

objective: Manage pediatric septic shock: antibiotics ideally within the first hour, fluid boluses reassessed after each, and epinephrine or norepinephrine (neither preferred first line), which may be started through a peripheral line rather than waiting for central access
secondaryObjectives: Give fluid boluses to children repeatedly while reassessing perfusion and urine output, and stop at signs of fluid overload
Judge a child's vital signs (heart rate, breathing rate, blood pressure) against norms for age, remembering that hypotension is a late sign of shock in children
Watch dehydrated or acutely ill children for hypo- or hypernatremia and hypoglycemia

sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 in SCCM's own guideline sheets: 'up to 40-60mL/kg in bolus fluid (10-20mL/kg per bolus) over the first hour' with intensive care available (Rec 17), titrated to clinical markers of cardiac output and stopped if 'signs of fluid overload develop'; overload named as 'clinical signs of pulmonary edema or new or worsening hepatomegaly'; reassessment markers 'heart rate, blood pressure, capillary refill time, level of consciousness, and urine output'; balanced crystalloids suggested over 0.9% saline (Rec 21). Vasoactive sheet: epinephrine rather than dopamine (Rec 28); no first-line choice between epinephrine and norepinephrine (Rec 30); no recommendation on peripheral initiation (Rec 31).

brief.situation: Handover at 14:00 in the pediatric ICU. Bed 6, a 4-year-old girl, 16 kg, two days of fever and vomiting, sent up from the ED. The ED placed one 22-gauge IV and gave 10 mL/kg of lactated Ringer's. Antibiotics are ordered and on the unit, not yet given; no blood culture was sent. A septic shock order set is active.
handover: Temperature 39.4, HR 167, BP 84/48, RR 34, SpO2 96% on room air.
Cool hands and feet, capillary refill about 4 seconds, sleepy but rousable. Little urine since morning.
The ED did not check a glucose or a lactate.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Boluses are ordered by size (10 or 20 mL/kg) and take minutes to run in. Reassess the child between boluses: the screen will not tell you when fluid stops helping.
Labs take minutes, the provider calls back, and the epinephrine takes minutes to work.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. The case ends at the attending's review two hours in, then a debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Total fluid this child can use before more fluid only congests her: 50 mL/kg including the ED's 10, inside the guideline's 40-60 mL/kg first-hour range. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

whatNow.question: What do you think is happening, and how will you decide whether to give the next bolus?

parts.label: What is happening
parts.criteria: Names septic shock (compensated, then decompensating) in a child, citing at least two of: tachycardia, capillary refill over 2 s with cool mottled skin, sleepiness, little urine, high lactate; notes that a normal blood pressure does not rule out shock in a child.
parts.modelAnswer: Septic shock: tachycardia, cool mottled skin with a capillary refill of 4 seconds, sleepiness, little urine and a high lactate. Her blood pressure was still normal at handover, but in children hypotension is a late sign.

parts.label: The next bolus
parts.criteria: Reassesses after every bolus (heart rate, capillary refill, mental state, urine output, blood pressure) and checks for overload (new or growing liver edge, crackles) before the next; gives 10-20 mL/kg boluses up to about 40-60 mL/kg; stops fluid at overload and asks for epinephrine or norepinephrine if shock persists; antibiotics within the hour.
parts.modelAnswer: Antibiotics now. Then 10 to 20 mL/kg at a time, and after each one look again: heart rate, capillary refill, how awake she is, urine, blood pressure, and the liver edge and the lungs. If perfusion improves and there is no liver growth or crackles, another bolus; if the liver grows or crackles appear, stop. If she is still in shock after about 40 mL/kg more, call for epinephrine through a peripheral IV.

reasoningCriteria.label: Written reasoning: named septic shock and how to decide on each bolus

expertPath.text: Look: compensated septic shock (HR 167, capillary refill 4 s, sleepy) with a normal BP, which in a child is a late sign. Glucose, culture, lactate.
First 20 mL/kg bolus. Call the attending: septic shock, ask them to come and for a vasoactive order if she stays in shock.
Culture drawn: antibiotics in at once. Low glucose: dextrose per the order set. Second IV.
Bolus in: reassess HR, capillary refill, mental state, urine, BP, liver edge and lungs. Still in shock, no overload: second 20 mL/kg.
Reassess: still in shock after 40 mL/kg more. Stop fluid; start epinephrine on its own peripheral IV and titrate every 5 min to perfusion.
Warm, capillary refill 2 s or less, passing urine at the review.

arrest.headline: Cardiac arrest from septic shock
arrest.body: Look at the first hour: when the antibiotics went in, when the attending was called, and how long she stayed in shock with nothing to hold the pressure.

stabilized.headline: Stabilized: septic shock treated on time
stabilized.body: Antibiotics in the first hour, boluses of 10-20 mL/kg each followed by a reassessment, fluid stopped before overload, and epinephrine through a peripheral line when fluid stopped helping. That is the expert path.

stabilizedLate.headline: Stabilized, by a slower route
stabilizedLate.body: She made it, but check the antibiotic time, the call, the boluses started without a reassessment, fluid given after the liver grew, and when the epinephrine started.

time_up.headline: Still in shock at the review
time_up.body: The perfusion never came back. The usual causes are a late antibiotic, fluid continued after it stopped helping, or no vasoactive.

scoring.modelReasoning: This is septic shock in a 4-year-old: tachycardia, cool mottled skin with a slow capillary refill, sleepiness, little urine and a high lactate, while the blood pressure is still normal for age. Antibiotics are time-critical (within an hour in septic shock) with a culture first only if it causes no delay. Fluid is given in 10-20 mL/kg boluses up to about 40-60 mL/kg in the first hour where intensive care is available, and every bolus is followed by a reassessment of heart rate, capillary refill, mental state, urine output and blood pressure, plus the liver edge and the lungs: new or growing hepatomegaly or crackles mean stop. Shock that persists after that needs epinephrine or norepinephrine, which the 2026 update (as relayed) supports starting peripherally rather than waiting for central access. Check and treat the glucose.

lateSign.ask: Her blood pressure is 84/48. Does a normal blood pressure for her age mean she is not in shock?

choices.label: No: hypotension is a late sign in children
Yes: shock means low blood pressure

lateSign.explain: No. Children hold their blood pressure by vasoconstriction and tachycardia until late; the cool skin, slow capillary refill, sleepiness and low urine say shock now. Hypotension at age 4 is a systolic below 78.

stopSign.ask: While this bolus runs: which finding at the next check would make you stop giving fluid?

choices.label: The liver edge is lower than before, or new crackles

stopSign.explain: New or worsening hepatomegaly or crackles mean she is not using more fluid; stop and move to a vasoactive. A fast heart rate and slow capillary refill without overload are reasons to consider another bolus, not to stop.

peripheralEpi.ask: If she is still in shock after 40 mL/kg more and has no central line, what will you ask for?

Wait for a central line first

peripheralEpi.explain: Start it peripherally. The 2020 panel made no recommendation on peripheral starts; the 2026 update, as relayed by secondary summaries, recommends peripheral access for vasoactives rather than waiting for central access. Use its own line and watch the site.
